pll.title: Permutation of the Last Layer
pll.desc:
PLL is the last step of the CFOP method. Once the first two layers are done and the top face is one color, it moves the last layer pieces into place. There are 21 algorithms: Aa, Ab, E, F, Ga, Gb, Gc, Gd, H, Ja, Jb, Na, Nb, Ra, Rb, T, Ua, Ub, V, Y and Z.

Since there are few cases and you use one in every solve, most people learn PLL before OLL. To recognize a case, look at the side faces: two corners of the same color next to each other (headlights) and blocks of two or three matching pieces are the clues. You may need to turn the top face before and after the algorithm (AUF); doing that without thinking makes PLL faster.

A common order: first the edge perms Ua, Ub, H and Z, then the corner perms Aa, Ab and E. G perms are harder to recognize, so they usually come last. Once you can recognize every case and execute it without pausing, you know PLL.

oll.title: Orientation of the Last Layer
oll.desc:
OLL is the third step of the CFOP method. After the first two layers it makes the top face one color; if you start with a white cross, it completes the yellow face. There are 57 cases, grouped by how many edges are already oriented on top: all four edges oriented, two edges oriented such as the L, T, P and W shapes, and the dot cases with none.

If you know 2-Look OLL, you already know 9 or 10 of them. Many algorithms are mirrors or inverses of each other, which makes them easier to memorize. Dot cases are usually the hardest and slowest, so most people leave them for last.

Starting with the cases whose edges are oriented and moving on to the T and L shapes is a good order. Picking algorithms that feel comfortable in your hands pays off in the long run.

f2l.title: First Two Layers
f2l.desc:
F2L is the second step of the CFOP method. After the cross you join a corner with its matching edge and insert them together into their slot as a pair. That is much faster than placing pieces one by one. There are 41 basic cases; the trainer shows each one for all four slots, 164 in total.

It helps to learn F2L intuitively before memorizing algorithms. If you understand why each case is solved the way it is, you can find your own solution in a new situation. Algorithms built on that base are also easier to remember.

The biggest gain in F2L comes from looking ahead: while you insert one pair, try to track where the next pair is. Avoiding unnecessary cube rotations matters a lot too. Later you can move on to VHLS or ZBLS, which also orient the top edges while inserting the last pair.

2_look_pll.title: 2-Look PLL
2_look_pll.desc:
2-Look PLL splits the permutation of the last layer into two steps: corners first, then edges. Six algorithms are enough: 2 for the corners and 4 for the edges.

In the first step you fix the corners. If one side face shows headlights (two corners of the same color), you use one algorithm; if there are none, you use the other. In the second step you place the edges with Ua, Ub, H and Z. If the corners are already in place the first step is skipped, and if the edges are, the second one is.

It is a little slower than full PLL, but starting with 6 algorithms instead of 21 makes learning much easier. Once you are comfortable with it, you can add full PLL one case at a time.

2_look_oll.title: 2-Look OLL
2_look_oll.desc:
2-Look OLL splits the orientation of the last layer into two steps: first you make a cross on top with the edges, then you orient the corners. There are 9 algorithms: 2 for the edges and 7 for the corners.

In the first step, if you see a line or an L shape on top, you do the matching algorithm; if there is only a dot, you do both one after the other. In the second step you orient the corners with the Sune, Antisune, H, T, L, Pi and U cases.

It is far easier to learn than the 57 algorithms of full OLL and a good bridge for beginners. Once you are comfortable, you can add the full OLL cases you meet most often one by one.

coll.title: Corners of the Last Layer
coll.desc:
COLL orients and permutes the last layer corners at once, when the top edges are already oriented. There are 40 cases in 7 groups based on how the corners look on top: Sune, Antisune, L, U, T, Pi and H.

After COLL the corners are always in place, so the only PLL left is an edge perm: Ua, Ub, H or Z. One time in 12 there is no PLL at all. You get short U perms instead of long G and N perms, which lowers your average time.

COLL is optional in CFOP: most people only use it when the cross on top comes for free. It is also a good step towards ZBLL, because the ZBLL groups follow the COLL groups.

ollcp.title: OLL and Corner Permutation
ollcp.desc:
OLLCP orients the last layer and places its corners at the same time, so it does OLL and corner permutation in one step. Each of the 57 OLL cases has 6 variants, 342 algorithms in total. Few people learn the whole set; most learn OLLCP only for certain OLL cases.

The benefit is like COLL: you reach PLL with the corners solved. But COLL only works when the edges are oriented, while OLLCP works for every OLL case.

Before starting OLLCP it helps to know full OLL and PLL well, and ideally to have tried COLL. Start with the cases you meet most often and that save the most time.

zbll.title: Zborowski-Bruchem Last Layer
zbll.desc:
ZBLL finishes the last layer with a single algorithm when all edges are oriented. There are 472 cases in 40 subgroups. The subgroups belong to the T, U, L, H, Pi, S and AS families, which match the COLL groups.

It fits the ZZ method best, because ZZ orients the edges at the very start. In CFOP it can follow ZBLS or VHLS. Learning the whole set is a big project that takes most people a long time.

The usual path is to learn COLL first and then add the ZBLL cases of each group little by little. The T and U groups are easier to recognize, so they usually come first.

zbls.title: Zborowski-Bruchem Last Slot
zbls.desc:
ZBLS orients the last layer edges while inserting the last F2L pair. This set has 42 cases, with one main algorithm for each. VHLS only covers short inserts; ZBLS covers many more last slot situations.

After ZBLS every top edge is oriented. That is a ready start for ZBLL, which solves the last layer in one step. Together ZBLS and ZBLL are one of the shortest routes through the last layer.

ZBLS is mostly used in ZZ and advanced CFOP. If you are not ready for the whole set, you can start with VHLS, which covers the most common situations.

wvls.title: Winter Variation Last Slot
wvls.desc:
WVLS (Winter Variation) is used when the last F2L pair is ready in the top layer and the top edges are oriented. While inserting the pair it also orients the top corners, so OLL is skipped. There are 27 cases in 4 groups based on how many corners are already oriented on top.

After WVLS you go straight to PLL. Because it only applies to one situation, you will not use it in every solve, but when it comes up it removes a whole step.

Before you start you should know full OLL and PLL and be able to track your F2L pairs comfortably. 27 cases is a small set; you recognize a case by the orientation of the top corners.

vhls.title: Vandenbergh-Harris Last Slot
vhls.desc:
VHLS orients the last layer edges while inserting the last F2L pair. It only covers short inserts, so it stays at 32 cases: 16 with the pair connected and 16 with it split. For longer situations you do normal F2L.

After VHLS only the OLL cases with oriented edges are left. The chance of skipping OLL rises from 1 in 216 to 1 in 27, and the remaining cases are usually shorter. If you also know COLL, VHLS and COLL together make a very strong last layer approach.

You can think of VHLS as a small part of ZBLS. Most cases are intuitive: you look at the orientation of the last edge and pick the right insert.

cmll.title: Corners of the Last Layer (Roux)
cmll.desc:
CMLL is the third step of the Roux method. After the two blocks you solve the last layer corners while ignoring the M slice completely. There are 42 cases in 8 groups: O, H, Pi, U, T, Sune, Antisune and L.

The difference from COLL is that CMLL may break the M slice. That freedom makes the algorithms generally shorter and faster.

Choosing good CMLL algorithms is one of the most direct ways to get faster with Roux. The last six edges step that follows CMLL is mostly intuitive and solved with M and U moves.

2_look_cmll.title: 2-Look CMLL
2_look_cmll.desc:
2-Look CMLL is the easy version of CMLL for people new to Roux. After the two blocks you solve the corners in two steps: orientation first, then permutation. There are 9 algorithms: 7 for orientation and 2 for permutation.

In the first step you orient the corners with Sune, Antisune and similar algorithms. In the second step you place them with an adjacent or a diagonal swap. Unlike COLL, breaking the M slice is allowed.

Once you are comfortable with the two blocks and the last six edges, you can move to full CMLL one case at a time.

oh_cmll.title: One-Handed CMLL
oh_cmll.desc:
One-Handed CMLL is a set of algorithms for the CMLL step of Roux chosen for solving with one hand. Same 42 cases and same 8 groups as normal CMLL; the difference is that the algorithms are easy to turn with one hand.

One-handed solvers avoid z and x rotations, because regripping the cube costs time. That is why the algorithms are mostly made of R, U and r moves. Left-handed solvers mirror them with L, U and l.

Normal CMLL algorithms also work one-handed, but they are slower. Learning CMLL two-handed first and then switching to the one-handed algorithms is a good order.

l6e_eo.title: Last Six Edges: Edge Orientation
l6e_eo.desc:
Edge orientation is the first part of the last six edges step in Roux. The last six edges are solved in three parts: orienting the edges, placing the left and right edges, and solving the last middle edges. All of it is done with M and U moves only.

This set has 11 cases, grouped by how many moves they take: 3, 5, 7 and 11 moves. The cases where you see an arrow shape on top are the shortest.

This is one of the most intuitive parts of Roux. To recognize a case, look at which edges are misoriented. With so few cases it is learned quickly and becomes a reflex with practice.

l6e_eolr.title: Edge Orientation and Left/Right Edges
l6e_eolr.desc:
EOLR is an advanced Roux technique that combines orienting the edges and placing the left and right edges into one step. There are 46 cases in 8 groups based on how the misoriented edges are spread between the top and the bottom.

The goal is to orient every edge while bringing the UL and UR edges to the bottom layer, then put them in place with M2. EOLR is mostly intuitive; tracking where the edges are and choosing the right M and U moves is enough.

Combining two steps lowers your move count and makes the solve flow. Before learning EOLR you should be comfortable doing edge orientation and the left and right edges separately.

2x2_cll.title: 2x2 Corners of the Last Layer
2x2_cll.desc:
CLL solves the last layer of the 2x2 in one step instead of the two steps of the beginner method. The bottom layer must be fully solved. There are 40 cases in 7 groups: Sune, Antisune, L, U, T, Pi and H.

The next step after CLL is EG-1 and EG-2. With them you do not need to finish the bottom layer; one face is enough. Together the three cover every situation after a face: CLL when the bottom layer is solved, EG-1 when the bottom corners have an adjacent swap, EG-2 when they have a diagonal swap.

To recognize a case, look at the corner colors on the top face and the patterns on the side faces. As recognition gets faster, CLL takes very little time.

2x2_eg1.title: 2x2 EG-1
2x2_eg1.desc:
EG-1 is a set of 40 cases learned after CLL. It covers the situations where the bottom corners have an adjacent swap. This is the most common situation, with a chance of 4 in 6.

CLL, EG-1 and EG-2 together cover every situation after one face is solved: CLL 1 in 6, EG-1 4 in 6, EG-2 1 in 6. Since EG-1 comes up most often, it is the set that saves the most time after CLL.

With EG-1 you only need to solve one face instead of the whole bottom layer. That lets you plan better during inspection and find shorter first steps.

2x2_eg2.title: 2x2 EG-2
2x2_eg2.desc:
EG-2 is the set of 40 cases usually learned last in the EG family. It covers the situations where the bottom corners have a diagonal swap. This is the least common situation, with a chance of 1 in 6.

Together with CLL and EG-1 it completes every 2x2 situation after one face. Because it comes up rarely it is usually learned last, but knowing all of EG means being ready for anything.

EG-2 gives you more freedom when choosing which face to solve during inspection. Recognizing the diagonal swap quickly directly affects how much this set helps.

2x2_pbl.title: Permutation of Both Layers
2x2_pbl.desc:
PBL is the last step of the Ortega method for the 2x2. In Ortega you first solve one face, then orient the opposite face, and finally permute both layers at once with PBL. There are 6 cases in total.

The cases differ in how adjacent and diagonal swaps are spread between the top and the bottom. The cases with a swap in only one layer are similar to the J and Y perms of the 3x3.

Ortega is the most common intermediate method before moving on to CLL and EG. PBL algorithms are short and comfortable to turn.

4x4_pll_parity.title: 4x4 PLL Parity
4x4_pll_parity.desc:
PLL parity is common on the 4x4, about once every two solves. An edge situation appears that cannot happen on a 3x3, because each 4x4 edge is made of two pieces that can pair up differently. OLL parity is a separate topic.

This set has 22 cases. The algorithms solve the parity together with the PLL in one step, which is faster than doing parity and PLL separately.

Start with the cases you meet most often and add the rare ones later. Well-chosen parity algorithms make a clear difference to your 4x4 times.

pyraminx_ll.title: Pyraminx Last Layer
pyraminx_ll.desc:
These algorithms solve the last layer of the Pyraminx with the layer by layer method. The method has two steps: first layer, then last layer. Three edges are left in the last layer, 5 cases in total.

The cases are simple and quick to learn; most algorithms are only a few moves. Recognition is easy too: you only look at three edges. A good start for anyone new to the Pyraminx.

Once you are comfortable with this method, you can move on to L4E or intuitive methods. These 5 cases stay useful either way.

pyraminx_l4e.title: Pyraminx Last 4 Edges
pyraminx_l4e.desc:
L4E is an advanced two-step Pyraminx method: first you build a V shape on the bottom, then you solve the remaining four edges in one step. This set has 35 cases in 5 groups based on the state of the edges.

A V shape is less restrictive than a full first layer, so it is easy to plan during inspection. To recognize a case, look at where the remaining edges are and how they are oriented.

Most fast Pyraminx solvers use this method. The algorithms are short, so choosing good fingertricks makes a big difference.

sarah_intermediate.title: Sarah's Intermediate (Skewb)
sarah_intermediate.desc:
Sarah's Intermediate is for Skewb solvers who want to go one step beyond the beginner method. With only 10 cases it is a good way to lower your times with little effort.

The method has three steps: solve one face, solve the opposite face with sledgehammer (R' F R F') and hedgeslammer (F R' F' R) triggers, then solve the centers. The cases are split into 3 groups by how many triggers they use.

It is a natural step towards Sarah's Advanced. Sledgehammer and hedgeslammer are the basic moves of the Skewb, and this method gets you used to them.

sarah_advanced.title: Sarah's Advanced (Skewb)
sarah_advanced.desc:
Sarah's Advanced reduces the Skewb solve to two steps: solve one face, then solve everything else in one step. This set has 93 cases for the second step, in 16 groups.

Most solutions are built on sledgehammer (R' F R F') and hedgeslammer (F R' F' R) triggers. To recognize a case, look at the pattern opposite the solved face and the colors on the side faces. Many cases are mirrors or inverses of each other.

Most fast Skewb solvers use this method. Learning the whole set takes time, but being able to plan the entire solve during inspection is a big advantage.

sq1_cube_shape.title: Square-1 Cube Shape
sq1_cube_shape.desc:
Cube shape is the first step of the Square-1 whatever method you use. The goal is to bring the scrambled shape back to a cube. This set has 169 cases, grouped from 1 to 7 by the number of slashes they need.

This step is unique to the Square-1; no other WCA puzzle has it. You recognize the shapes of the top and bottom layers and apply the right sequence. The shapes have names like kite, scallop, square and mushroom.

To recognize a case, look at the number and shape of the pieces in the top and bottom layers. At first you can follow a general path such as star, square, cube; later you learn the shortest solutions directly.

sq1_cp.title: Square-1 Corner Permutation
sq1_cp.desc:
Corner permutation comes after cube shape and orientation and puts every corner in place. There are 8 cases: combinations of an adjacent swap, a diagonal swap or a solved state on the top and bottom. They are split into 3 groups by the top layer.

An adjacent swap means two neighboring corners trade places; a diagonal swap means two opposite corners do. To recognize a case, look at the corner colors.

You can recognize the corner permutation case even during inspection, which makes planning easier.

sq1_csp.title: Square-1 Cube Shape Parity
sq1_csp.desc:
CSP is an advanced technique that handles parity in the cube shape step. Its main benefit is that parity is detected during inspection, before the timer runs. That is much faster than a separate parity step inside the solve. This set has 179 cases, grouped by the number of slashes.

During inspection you look at where the corners and edges are to tell whether there is parity. If there is, you do the cube shape with a special algorithm that also fixes parity. If not, you use your normal cube shape algorithm.

CSP removes the parity step from the solve completely. It does require spotting parity quickly during inspection, which improves with practice.

sq1_eo.title: Square-1 Edge Orientation
sq1_eo.desc:
Edge orientation comes after cube shape and corner orientation and turns every edge the right way. When it is done, the colors of the top and bottom faces are fully correct. There are 7 cases.

The cases differ in how many misoriented edges are on the top and the bottom. Recognition is easy: you check whether the top and bottom colors of the edges are right. The algorithms are usually short.

This step is also the base for OBL, which orients both layers at once.

sq1_ep.title: Square-1 Edge Permutation
sq1_ep.desc:
Edge permutation is usually the last step of the Square-1 and puts every edge in place. There are 40 cases in 8 groups based on the top layer.

With parity the normal algorithms do not work and you need one that also fixes parity (unless you used CSP). Learning algorithms that solve both together is more efficient than doing them separately.

To recognize a case, look at where the edges are. Picking the right algorithm quickly directly affects your Square-1 times.

sq1_obl.title: Square-1 Orient Both Layers
sq1_obl.desc:
OBL is an advanced technique that orients the corners and edges of both layers at once. This set has 185 cases, grouped by the number of slashes. The simpler approach orients corners and edges in separate steps; OBL does both in one.

To recognize a case you have to look at the corner and edge colors on the top and bottom faces at the same time. That is harder than recognizing them separately, but it settles in with practice.

Because OBL removes a whole step, it saves time in every solve. It helps to be comfortable with corner and edge orientation as separate steps first.

advanced_f2l.title: Advanced F2L
advanced_f2l.desc:
Advanced F2L covers the F2L situations where the pieces sit in bad places: the corner or the edge is trapped in another slot, sometimes both. There are 54 cases; the trainer shows each one for all four slots, 216 in total. The cases are split into 3 groups by which piece is trapped.

In normal F2L you would take the piece out first and then build the pair. These algorithms do both in one flow and skip the wasted moves. Once basic F2L feels easy, this is the next step.

sbls.title: Second Block Last Slot
sbls.desc:
SBLS inserts the last pair of the second block in the Roux method. There are 65 cases, split into 6 groups by where the corner is: three orientations on the top layer and three on the bottom.

The last slot of the second block is one of the places where Roux solves lose the most time. If you know these cases, you go straight to CMLL once the block is done.

eo4a.title: Edge Orientation (4a)
eo4a.desc:
EO4A is the first part of the Roux last six edges step (L6E): it fixes the orientation of the six edges. This set has 9 cases. L6E-EO shows the same step split into 11 cases; here each case is named by how the flipped edges are spread between top and bottom.

Once the edges are oriented, only a short step solved with M and U moves is left.

anti_pll.title: Anti PLL
anti_pll.desc:
Anti PLL solves, with one algorithm, the cases where all four last layer edges are flipped and the corners are oriented. Doing OLL there would leave a PLL; Anti PLL finishes both at once. There are 22 cases.

Anti PLL is part of 1LLL. Together with PLL and ZBLL it makes up the most studied parts of the last layer.

sv.title: Summer Variation
sv.desc:
SV is used when the last F2L pair goes in with R U' R' and the top edges are oriented. It orients the top corners while inserting the pair, so OLL is skipped. There are 27 cases.

It is the sibling of Winter Variation (WVLS): WVLS covers the pair that goes in with R U R', SV the one that goes in with R U' R'. Together they are the best known way to skip OLL at the last slot.

ell.title: Edges of the Last Layer
ell.desc:
ELL finishes the remaining edges in one step when the last layer corners are solved: it fixes both their orientation and their position. There are 25 cases.

It is the last step of methods that solve the corners first. In CFOP it helps when the corners happen to be solved after OLL.

1lll.title: One-Look Last Layer
1lll.desc:
1LLL solves the last layer with one algorithm, whatever state it is in. The full set has thousands of cases, so nobody memorizes all of them; this category shows the part of the set outside PLL, ZBLL and Anti PLL.

For the whole of 1LLL, add PLL, ZBLL and Anti PLL to this category. The cases are split into 49 groups. Picking one group and working through it slowly is far more effective than opening them all at once.

vls.title: Valk Last Slot
vls.desc:
VLS orients the last layer while inserting the last F2L pair; only PLL is left after it. It is named after Mats Valk. This set has 189 cases, split into 7 groups by which top edges are oriented.

Winter Variation is a part of VLS. VLS is a big set; most people learn WVLS first and then add the VLS groups that come up most often.

cls.title: Corners Last Slot
cls.desc:
CLS is used when the last slot edge is already in place and the top edges are oriented. It inserts the last corner and orients every top corner at the same time, so OLL is skipped. This set has 97 cases.

The cases are split into 4 groups by the corner: trapped in its slot, or on top with the cross color facing front, right or up. After CLS you go straight to PLL.

fruf.title: F <R,U> F'
fruf.desc:
FRUF algorithms start with F, use only R and U moves in the middle and end with F'. The case is the state after the F move: you learn the R and U part in the middle. There are 42 cases.

The part made of R and U moves only is fast and easy to turn. That makes this set a good addition for anyone who wants to finish part of the last layer with smooth, short algorithms.

2x2_ortega_oll.title: 2x2 Ortega OLL
2x2_ortega_oll.desc:
In the Ortega method you complete the top face with one algorithm after solving the first face. There are 7 cases: Sune, Antisune, H, Pi, U, T and L.

The last step of Ortega is PBL, which places the corners of both layers together. On 2x2 this is the most recommended path after the beginner method.

4x4_oll_parity.title: 4x4 OLL Parity
4x4_oll_parity.desc:
On 4x4 a single edge pair can end up flipped on the last layer, which is impossible on 3x3. This is called OLL parity and is fixed with a dedicated algorithm.

This set has 2 cases. Basic is short and common but also moves the last layer corners. Pure fixes only the flipped edge and leaves everything else in place.

faq.q: What is Zkt Timer?
faq.a: Zkt Timer is one of the most advanced online Rubik's cube timer platforms. It measures your speedcubing solve times with millisecond precision, provides official WCA scramble algorithms, detailed statistics and performance analysis. Features include live race rooms, smart cube support, and an algorithm trainer.

faq.q: How does Zkt Timer work?
faq.a: Sign up and start right away. Core features like the timer, statistics, online races and the trainer are available. Upgrade to Pro membership for additional premium features.

faq.q: Which cube types are supported?
faq.a: Zkt Timer supports all official WCA categories: 2x2, 3x3, 4x4, 5x5, 6x6, 7x7; Pyraminx, Megaminx, Skewb, Square-1, Clock; 3x3 One-Handed, 3x3 Blindfolded and more. Official WCA scramble algorithms are used for each category.

faq.q: Can I use it offline?
faq.a: Yes! Zkt Timer works offline thanks to PWA technology. After installing the app via your browser's 'Add to Home Screen' option, you can use the timer without internet. Your data automatically syncs when you reconnect.

faq.q: Is it an official WCA timer?
faq.a: Zkt Timer uses official WCA scramble algorithms and is built for training purposes. Physical Stackmat Timers are required for official WCA competitions. Zkt Timer is ideal for practice, training, and statistics tracking.

faq.q: Which devices are supported?
faq.a: Zkt Timer works on all modern browsers. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS are supported. It can be installed as a PWA on your phone. It's also compatible with Smart Cubes (GAN, MoYu) and Stackmat Timer.

faq.q: Is my data safe?
faq.a: Yes, all solve records and account information are stored securely. Your data is kept both on the server and in your browser's local database. You can delete your account and all data at any time.

faq.q: How can I join online races?
faq.a: Create an account, then join open race rooms or create private rooms with friends from the 'Rooms' section. Real-time races are held.

faq.q: How can I track WCA competitions?
faq.a: Browse all WCA Rubik's cube competitions worldwide from the 'Competitions' section. Each competition's detail page shows schedule, competitor list, events and live results. Connect your WCA account to see your personal schedule for competitions you're registered for.

faq.q: How do I connect a smart cube?
faq.a: Zkt Timer supports GAN, Giiker, and Particula smart cubes via Bluetooth. On mobile, enable Bluetooth and use the Capacitor BLE plugin; on web browsers, use Chrome or Edge which support Web Bluetooth. Open the Smart Cube menu from the timer, press Scan, and pair with your device. Once connected, the timer auto-starts and stops based on the cube state.

faq.q: Does Zkt Timer support Stackmat Timer?
faq.a: Yes. Connect your Stackmat Timer via the audio input (3.5mm jack). In the timer settings, select StackMat as the input type, then choose the correct audio input device. The timer will detect your Stackmat signals automatically.

faq.q: What is the Algorithm Trainer?
faq.a: The Algorithm Trainer helps you practice OLL, PLL, F2L, ZBLL and other cube algorithms. It shows each algorithm as a 2D pattern or on a 3D cube, keeps your times per algorithm and can put the cases you are slow on or miss first. You can collect your algorithms in sets and share them, and follow every move with a smart cube.

faq.q: What are OLL and PLL?
faq.a: OLL (Orientation of the Last Layer) and PLL (Permutation of the Last Layer) are the final two steps of the CFOP speedsolving method. OLL has 57 algorithms that orient the last layer; PLL has 21 algorithms that permute the pieces. Mastering these is essential for sub-20 solves.

faq.q: What does Pro membership give me?
faq.a: Zkt Timer Pro unlocks advanced statistics, unlimited sessions, PDF export of your algorithms and stats, access to all algorithm trainers, premium themes, and priority support. It's a one-time or recurring purchase depending on the plan.

faq.q: Can I import data from csTimer or Twisty Timer?
faq.a: Yes. Zkt Timer supports data import from csTimer, Twisty Timer, and its own previous export formats. Go to Settings > Data > Import, select the source format, and upload your export file. All solves, sessions, and metadata are preserved.

faq.q: How do I back up my data?
faq.a: Go to Settings > Data > Export. Zkt Timer generates a JSON file containing all your solves, sessions, and settings. Store this file safely — you can re-import it on any device. Signed-in users also get automatic cloud sync.

faq.q: Which scramble algorithm does Zkt Timer use?
faq.a: Zkt Timer uses the same scramble engine as cstimer, the de facto standard in speedcubing. This includes WCA-compliant random-state scramblers for 2x2, 3x3, 4x4, Pyraminx, Megaminx, Skewb, Square-1, Clock, and more. All scrambles meet WCA regulations.

faq.q: What is Battle mode?
faq.a: Battle mode is a 1v1 competitive mode on one shared screen, and it works on phones, tablets and computers. Two cubers race side-by-side with independent start timing, penalty tracking (+2, DNF), round-by-round scoring, and a review modal to examine each round. Each player can also connect their own smart cube. Perfect for quick duels with a friend.

faq.q: Can I delete my account?
faq.a: Yes, completely. Go to Settings > Account > Danger Zone > Delete Account. This permanently removes all your solves, sessions, profile data, and WCA link. The action is irreversible. Export your data first if you want to keep a backup.

faq.q: Do I need to pay to use Zkt Timer?
faq.a: You can sign up and use the core experience at no cost: the timer, WCA scrambles, statistics, online race rooms, leaderboards, and the algorithm trainer. Pro membership unlocks advanced statistics, unlimited sessions, PDF export, smart-cube trainer modes, premium themes, and priority support. There are no ads.

faq.q: Is there an iOS or Android app?
faq.a: Yes. Zkt Timer is available natively on the iOS App Store and Google Play Store. The apps include smart cube Bluetooth support, offline mode, push notifications, and native performance. You can also install the web app as a PWA.

faq.q: What is inspection mode?
faq.a: Inspection mode is the 15-second countdown before each solve, matching WCA regulations. During inspection, you examine the scramble without touching the cube. An audible 8-second and 12-second warning plays, and starting after 15 seconds incurs a +2 penalty (17+ seconds is DNF).

faq.q: Are stats tracked separately for different cube types?
faq.a: Yes. Zkt Timer buckets stats by (cube type, scramble subset). Your 3x3 averages, 2x2 personal bests, and Pyraminx times are all tracked independently. The Stats page lets you filter by cube type and time range.

faq.q: How does Zkt Timer work without internet?
faq.a: As a PWA, Zkt Timer caches all app files after the first visit. You can time solves, generate scrambles, and view cached stats fully offline. When you reconnect, pending solves are automatically synced to the server via Background Sync API.

faq.q: What is the PLL recognition trainer?
faq.a: The PLL recognition trainer drills your ability to identify the correct PLL case by sight and type its letter name from the keyboard — no solving required. It includes a guided multi-step quest, a two-sided recognition guide covering every angle, an adaptive queue that focuses on your weak cases, and a glossary. It runs as a separate, keyboard-based mode.

faq.q: What is the cross efficiency trainer?
faq.a: The efficiency trainer helps you build more efficient Cross, XCross and EOCross solutions. It analyzes your moves, shows optimal or near-optimal solutions and helps you cut move count for faster, smoother solves. With a smart cube connected it can follow your real solution live.

faq.q: What are the keyboard shortcuts?
faq.a: Space starts and stops the timer. Escape resets the inspection countdown while it is running. For the last solve: 1 clears the penalty, 2 adds a +2, 3 marks it DNF, Alt+Z deletes it. Alt+I toggles inspection. Change the puzzle with Alt and a number: Alt+2 through Alt+7 for 2x2 up to 7x7, Alt+P for Pyraminx, Alt+M for Megaminx, Alt+C for Clock, Alt+S for Skewb. On a Mac, Command works instead of Ctrl.

faq.q: How do I use Zkt Timer on a desktop?
faq.a: The menus at the top select your session, puzzle and timer type, with the scramble right below them. Hold space and release to start, press again to stop. Your recent solves, your averages and the solve analysis sit in modules beside the timer, and you can drag the modules wherever you like. Click any time to open its detail window, where you can add a penalty, see the scramble or delete the solve.

faq.q: How do I reach the menus on mobile?
faq.a: There is a thin notch on the left and right edge of the screen. Tap the right notch or swipe left from it to open navigation: timer, stats, trainer, rooms and the rest live there. The left notch opens quick settings. Press and hold a notch to move it up or down. Both notches hide while a solve is running.

faq.q: Where are the settings?
faq.a: Tap your profile picture in the top right and choose General settings. Timer layout, inspection, sounds, theme, smart cube and data settings are all there. On mobile, the notch on the left edge also opens quick settings for the ones you change often.

faq.q: How do sessions work?
faq.a: A session is a separate list of solves. Use the session menu above the timer to create one, switch between them, rename one or merge two together. Averages are calculated per session.

faq.q: How do I add a penalty or delete a solve?
faq.a: Tap the time in your solve list and use the +2, DNF and delete options in the window that opens. The +2 and DNF buttons under the timer always apply to your last solve. On desktop, 2, 3 and Alt+Z do the same for the last solve.

credits.title: Zkt Timer
credits.intro_1: Zkt Timer is a project born out of my own needs as someone actively involved in speedcubing. I've been cubing for a long time, and after I started competing, I realized that the tools I was using were falling short in certain areas. I needed a more flexible and more powerful system, especially around analysis, the trainer, and the overall user experience.
credits.intro_2: With that need in mind, I started building a timer for myself, leveraging my software background. My initial goal was simple: to create a system that covered my own use case and that I had full control over. But as development progressed, the project grew. It evolved from a simple timer into a much more comprehensive system with analysis tools, trainer modules, smart cube integration, synchronization, and many other components.
credits.intro_3: Over a roughly nine-month period, the project evolved significantly. What started as a web application gradually expanded to mobile platforms and became a multi-platform app. Throughout this process, my work wasn't just about adding new features; the real focus was revisiting systems again and again, redesigning some of them from scratch, and making sure all the pieces worked together coherently.
credits.intro_4: Today, Zkt Timer is a system that began as the result of a single need, grew over time, and is still being actively developed.
credits.builder_ibrhyyme: The person who designs and develops Zkt Timer.
credits.credits_intro_1: While building Zkt Timer, I actively benefited from existing projects in the speedcubing ecosystem. There is a strong open-source culture that has grown over the years, and I studied many of these projects in detail; I ran some of them, and read others line by line to understand how they worked.
credits.credits_intro_2: Throughout this process, I learned different things from different places. Some projects guided me on the technical side — for example in scramble generation or solver approaches. Others helped me understand what works well on the trainer and user experience side. Sometimes it was an algorithmic idea, sometimes a data model, sometimes the overall approach of a system that became a reference for me.
credits.credits_intro_3: Rather than taking these pieces as-is, I revisited each of them so they would fit Zkt Timer's own structure. I rewrote most systems from scratch; I simplified some and extended others. Bringing approaches from different sources together under a single architecture, in a coherent and interoperable way, was the most critical part of this process.
credits.credits_intro_4: The resulting structure isn't tied to a single source. Rather, it emerged from combining and rebuilding approaches learned from different projects.
credits.credits_belief: I believe this: moving something forward isn't just about adding something new; it's about properly understanding the work done before you and making an honest contribution on top of it. That's why it matters to me to acknowledge everyone who has had a direct or indirect impact on this project.
credits.credits_outro: The projects and developers named below played different roles in shaping Zkt Timer. Some were the starting point of an idea, some helped me solve a problem, and some made it possible for me to see a better approach.
credits.credits_thanks: My deepest respect and gratitude to all of them.
credits.inspiration_desc: The projects below served as references in different ways throughout Zkt Timer's development. Each entry states two things: what was taken from that project, and what was built on top of it.
credits.inspiration_cubedesk: My strongest reference on the software architecture side of Zkt Timer. How React + SSR, Node.js + GraphQL, PostgreSQL + Prisma and Redis fit together inside a cubing platform was worked out by studying cubedesk by kash. It guided the service organisation and folder structure. Its influence was not limited to the server side: the interface language cubedesk established was also a reference for the timer screen layout, the solve list and the module arrangement. Where we part ways: cubedesk is a web app. I wanted the same codebase to ship to iOS and Android through Capacitor, so I rebuilt the SSR layer, the session handling and the cross-device sync to carry the native side as well.
credits.inspiration_cstimer: The foundation of scramble generation. The scramble algorithms and subset structure for the puzzle types, the min2phase Kociemba solver and the group theory library were built with reference to csTimer and min2phase by cs0x7f. While moving this code from JavaScript to TypeScript it was restructured around a registry-based generator architecture; every puzzle type now registers its own generator, and the client and the server can produce the same scramble. On top of that, more than 40 CFOP, Roux, Mehta and ZZ subsets, my own 2D renderers for Square-1 and Clock, and a Web Worker layer that runs the heavy solvers without freezing the interface were added.
credits.inspiration_cubedex: One of my main references for the user experience side of the Trainer module. How a smart cube connects into a drilling flow was worked out by studying Pau Oliva Fora's project. In Zkt Timer this structure was split into four separate modes (Standard, Smart Cube, Recognition, Efficiency); per-algorithm statistics were kept, the queue order was made to adapt to the cases a user is weak at, and 2D and 3D pattern visualisation plus PDF export for printing algorithm sheets were added.
credits.inspiration_cubingapp: A large portion of the algorithm collection used in the Trainer came from the cubingapp dataset created by spencerchubb and was adapted to Zkt Timer's data model. The setup algorithms were regenerated with my own scripts, the pattern images were run through my own rendering pipeline, the collection was split into 31 categories and extended with algorithms of my own.
credits.inspiration_rubikssolverdemo: The starting point for the Cross, XCross, EOCross and F2L pair solver logic. The coordinate-based IDA* implementations developed by or18 were a fundamental reference in the design of Zkt Timer's solver system. The work in this module was porting and adaptation: the solvers were moved into a Web Worker architecture and wired into a step-by-step solution interface. The mathematics behind the algorithm belongs to or18.
credits.inspiration_letscube: The conceptual basis for 1v1 rooms and the friendly-race format comes from this project. How a synchronised, shared solve model is built was worked out by studying coder13's work. Zkt Timer's room system was written from scratch on top of that idea, and the following were added as things I considered missing in LetsCube: smart cube support inside rooms, live chat, spectator mode, room moderation and user banning, a 1v1 duel mode, and a Socket.IO layer that broadcasts across multiple servers through Redis.
credits.inspiration_competitorgroups: A project built so competitors can follow their own groups and assignments at WCA competitions, and it does that job very well. I did not want competitors to have to visit a separate site for this information, so the same experience was brought inside Zkt Timer. A competitor's own schedule, their judging and scrambling assignments, their per-event personal bests and their round results are now gathered on a single screen. The layout of the group screens took shape under the influence of this project.
credits.inspiration_wcalive: A platform built for following WCA competitions live, and one that solves round-by-round result flow genuinely well. The WCA Software Team's work was the direct source for the structural approach of the WCA Live integration in Zkt Timer. The ZKT competition platform itself was written from scratch for Zkt Timer: registration, scorecard entry, batch entry mode, round management, judge, scrambler and runner assignment, national record tracking, delegate management, A/B day-split competitions and WCIF generation. What was taken from wca-live is the logic of the delegate workflow.
credits.inspiration_rubikcube: The interactive 3D cube on the landing page was ported one-to-one from this project by Dev-tanay. The source was written against Three.js r95; the changed APIs were adapted while moving it to r125 and the code was converted to TypeScript. The class structure and method names stayed the same as the source. My addition was wiring the cube into Zkt Timer's timer: scramble generation, solve detection and timing. In this entry the skeleton of the code belongs to Dev-tanay.
credits.inspiration_pllrecognition: The direct basis for the PLL Recognition Trainer module. The keyboard-driven PLL recognition practice, the two-sided recognition guide and the adaptive repetition logic came from Roman Strakhov's project. The source was written in Vue; the module was rewritten in React and TypeScript. During the rewrite the recognition guide was completed to cover all 73 cases, and an on-device history layer, a glossary view and a 13-step guided quest were added. The module is roughly four times the size of the source today.

credits.libraries_cubingjs: The core library used for smart cube state tracking, WCA notation, and KPattern matching. Developed by Lucas Garron and the cubing.js contributors.
credits.libraries_ganweb: The library that provides Bluetooth connection management and gyroscope/motion logic for GAN smart cubes. The Smart Cube module is built on top of this library.

credits.opensource_text: Zkt Timer is built on top of hundreds of open-source packages, including React, Apollo, Prisma, and Three.js. The full list of dependencies can be found in the package.json file. A heartfelt thanks to everyone who has built and maintained these libraries over the years.
credits.community_text: To the WCA and the global speedcubing community. A remarkable worldwide community has been built around a single puzzle. The real reason Zkt Timer means anything is that it gets to be a part of this community.

credits.originals_desc: This section covers the features designed and developed for Zkt Timer. Each one grew out of the platform's own needs and the feedback that came from its users.
credits.original_notifications: Zkt Timer generates automatic notifications for the competitions you follow. Registration opening, publication of groups and assignments, results being entered and records being broken are all delivered as notifications, and a countdown runs up to the competition date. The system runs as scheduled jobs on the server and produces both in-app and push notifications.
credits.original_radar: Calculates in advance which records could fall at a competition you are attending. The competitor list, the event schedule and the current national records are compared to determine which records are at risk, and the result is shown on the competition page.
credits.original_native: Zkt Timer ships as a native app on iOS and Android. Smart cube connectivity runs through a native BLE layer, and accelerometer and haptic support are provided through native plugins. Edge gestures, safe areas and keyboard behaviour are handled separately for each platform.
credits.original_offline: Solves can be recorded, sessions can be opened and statistics can be viewed with no internet connection. When the connection returns, pending solves are queued and reconciled with the server, conflicts are resolved, and duplicate records are filtered out by fingerprint.
credits.original_battle: A mode designed for mobile that lets two people compete head to head on the same device. Players start independently, penalties and scores are tracked separately, and round history is stored in detail.
credits.original_cubercard: A shareable card that turns profile information into a single image. Avatar, name, competition count, medals and WCA records appear on the card. It hooks into the native share sheet on mobile and into a direct download on desktop.

getting-started.title: Getting started
body: You can use Zkt Timer in a browser or through the iOS and Android apps. With an account your solves are backed up to the server, so your data survives losing the device. Seeing that history on every device you sign in on comes with Pro; without it, your solves stay on the device that made them.

You can also try it without an account. Signed out, the timer, your solves and the trainer all work; the times stay on that device only. If you sign up later, the app offers to move those solves into your account.

On desktop the timer sits in the middle of the screen: three menus at the top (session, cube type and timer type), with the scramble and the time below them. In the default layout your solve list and stat modules sit in the columns on either side, and you can move the modules wherever you like.

Settings are split into eight sections: Timer, Input & Devices, Smart Cube, Scramble, Appearance, Colors, Data and Language. If you are not sure which section holds the setting you want, use the search box inside settings.

timer.title: Timer
body: Hold the space bar, let go when the timer turns green, and the time starts. Press any key to stop. On mobile you press and release the middle of the screen.
With inspection on, a 15-second countdown runs before the time starts. Following the WCA rule, going past 15 seconds is a +2 and going past 17 is a DNF. Escape cancels the countdown.

A scramble is generated after every solve. Tap the scramble to copy it, and use the arrows beside it to move between the previous and next scrambles. In the 3D scramble preview, the three faces you cannot see (back, left and bottom) are also shown floating beside the cube, so you can check the whole scramble at a glance.
You pick the timer type from the menu at the top. These are the supported inputs:
notes: Manual entry sits in the same menu and works differently: no stopwatch runs, you type the time in yourself.
Smart cube, GAN Timer and QiYi Timer require Pro inside rooms. On the timer page all three are open to everyone.

solves.title: Solves and sessions
body: The list under the timer shows the solves in that session. Tapping a time opens the detail window: you can add a penalty, look at the scramble and the solve breakdown, or delete the solve.
The +2 and DNF buttons right below the timer always apply to your last solve.

The solves page gathers every solve into one list. You can filter by time range, by penalty, by whether the solve was done with a smart cube and by whether it was imported, and sort by time or by date.
The same page has multi-select: tick several solves and delete them in one go.

A session is a list you keep your solves apart in: warm-up, 3x3 practice, one-handed and so on. You switch between them from the session menu at the top. On the sessions page you create a session, rename it, drag to reorder, merge two of them, or select several and delete them. Averages are worked out per session.

stats.title: Statistics
body: The stats page offers two views. The overview shows where you stand across every cube type, your activity heat map and how many solves you do per day.
Picking a cube type opens the view for that cube: your best single and averages, a timeline, consistency by hour of day, a solve calendar and the phase breakdown of solves done with a smart cube.

The filters at the top choose the session, the cube type, the subset (3x3 One-Handed, for instance) and how many recent solves to look at. Your choices are written into the address bar, so you can share a link to a particular view.
notes: Two sections built on smart cube data come with Pro: average phase times and case-by-case statistics.

trainer.title: Trainer
body: The trainer is for practicing algorithms and has two parts: Trainers and Algorithm Sets. Trainers holds three trainers: Algorithm Trainer, PLL Recognition, and Cross and XCross. Time and success rate are kept per algorithm, so the cases you are weak on stand out.
steps: Algorithm Trainer: you practice the algorithms you pick from categories like OLL, PLL, F2L and ZBLL. Use Add to set to put an algorithm you like in one of your sets.

Smart Cube mode: switch to it with the Standard / Smart Cube toggle at the top of the Algorithm Trainer. Connect the cube and it reads your turns and sees whether you executed the algorithm correctly.
Cross and XCross: compares how many moves you used for the cross against the shortest solution.
PLL recognition: you type the case's letter on the keyboard, no solving needed. It measures how fast you recognise.
Algorithm Sets: collect the algorithms you want to practice in your own sets and share them with friends. From Community Sets at the top of My Sets you can find sets others shared and save them.
notes: The PLL recognition mode has its own history, settings and glossary; the history page lets you compare earlier rounds.
Drilling algorithms with a smart cube, and downloading algorithms with their alternatives as a PDF, both require Pro.

smart-cube.title: Smart cube
body: Zkt Timer recognises smart cubes from these brands:
Once connected, the cube's state appears on screen in 3D. The timer starts when you turn the cube and stops on its own when the cube is solved.
steps: Turn the cube on and keep it near your device.
On the timer page, pick Smart Cube from the timer type menu.
Press Scan and choose your cube from the list.
On the first connection, set the cube to solved and sync it.
notes: In a browser this needs Web Bluetooth: use Chrome or Edge, Safari does not support it. The iOS and Android apps have no such limit.
If the cube on screen drifts from the real one, set the cube to solved and sync again. If the connection drops, power-cycle the cube and scan again.
Step-by-step analysis after a solve comes with Pro: Cross, F2L, OLL and PLL times, move count, turns per second and a replay of the solve.
If the scan cannot find your cube, press Show all devices on the screen that opens; every Bluetooth device nearby is listed.

A connected cube stays connected as you move between the timer, rooms and the trainer, so you do not have to pair it again on each page. If the app or browser tab stays in the background for five minutes, the connection closes to save battery.

As you turn the cube, the scramble's moves are ticked off one by one. If you make a wrong move, the moves needed to fix it are shown. When the scramble is done, "Ready to Start" appears and the timer starts with your first move.

In Settings > Smart Cube you set the size of the cube view, how finely the solve is split into steps, and extra time added to every smart cube solve. On desktop, add the Live Phases module to watch phase times come in while you solve a 3x3.

lift-to-start.title: Magnet Timer
body: Magnet Timer starts the timer when you lift the cube and stops it when you put the cube down on the table, without touching the screen. The phone lies flat on the table and the cube rests at the phone's rear camera end.

The phone's compass sensor picks up the magnets inside the cube, so you need a magnetic cube; most cubes sold today are magnetic. You also need the Zkt Timer iOS or Android app. Magnet Timer is not available in a browser or in rooms.

Not every phone's sensor is fast enough for this. On unsupported phones Magnet Timer is not in the list, or the screen says "This device's sensor is too slow". If you cannot see it, update the app first.
steps: Lay the phone flat on the table. Open the timer types from the left notch and choose Magnet Timer.
Put the cube right next to the phone at its rear camera end. It does not have to touch the phone.
Leave the cube still. You are ready when the time turns green and "Lift to start the timer" appears under it.
Lift the cube and the timer starts at that moment. When you finish, put the cube down on the table and the timer stops.
notes: Magnet Timer needs Pro and is still in beta.
With inspection on, the first lift starts inspection. Put the cube back and lift it again when you are ready; the timer starts at that moment. +2 and DNF apply as usual.

After a solve, lifting the cube from its spot does not start a new one; the cube has to be away for a few seconds first. That way picking the cube up to scramble it never starts the timer by accident. If the screen says "Pick up the cube, scramble it, then put it back", do exactly that.

With Magnet Timer, touching the screen neither starts nor stops the timer, so it is fine if your hand brushes the screen while you place or grab the cube. To abandon an inspection, swipe up on the screen. If the timer does not stop when you put the cube down, press and hold the screen for a second; the time stops at the moment you pressed.
If the screen says "Move the cube away from the phone", do that. If the message stays, press Reset baseline while the phone is still; the phone then learns its surroundings without the cube again.
With Phone upside down in Quick Settings you can turn the phone around and put the cube between you and the phone. The timer screen and the side menus turn 180 degrees.

Without a magnetic cube you can use Drop to Stop with the Touch timer: when you finish, put the cube or your hands down on the table, and the phone feels the impact and stops the timer. Turn it on at the top of Quick Settings and set its sensitivity to suit your table there. It needs Pro.

mobile.title: Using it on mobile
body: On mobile the menus live in thin notches at the edges of the screen. Tap the right-hand notch or swipe left from it: the timer, stats, trainer, rooms and the other pages are there. The left notch opens the quick settings.
Press and hold a notch to move it up or down. Notches hide while the timer is running, so they cannot be opened by accident.
notes: To go back from a page, swipe right from the left edge of the screen. It is switched off on the timer page, where the left edge belongs to the quick settings notch. In the Android app the system's own back button does this instead.

customize.title: Personalization
body: In Settings > Colors you choose the colors of the puzzles. Cubes from 2x2 to 7x7, Square-1, Clock and FTO each have their own color group. The colors you pick are used in the scramble image, the smart cube view and the other puzzle drawings across the app.

In Settings > Appearance you can put an image or a video behind the timer. PNG, JPG or an MP4 of up to 40 MB can be uploaded, and the video pauses while the timer runs. Show background is set per device, so you can keep it on at your desk and off on your phone.
In the same section, Solve list colors changes the color of the times and records in the list.

On desktop you place the modules on the timer screen wherever you like: the left column, the right column, the strip under the timer or any empty spot. A module dropped on an empty spot stays there, floating.
steps: Drag a module by its header and drop it into a column, the bottom strip or an empty spot.
Click the module's name to swap it for another module; remove it with the X button.
Press the plus button to add a new module.
Resize columns and floating modules by dragging their edges.
notes: Putting your own image or video behind the timer needs Pro.
To put the modules back where they started, use the Reset layout button in Settings > Appearance. Modules cannot be moved while the timer is running.
On mobile the modules sit in two slots under the timer; you choose which ones show in Quick Settings.

rooms.title: Rooms
body: Rooms are for solving the same scramble as your friends. Everyone gets the same scramble and the times show up on everyone's screen.

A room holds 8 people by default and the owner can raise that to 16. You can make a room private and put a password on it. Everything from 2x2 to 7x7 is supported, plus Clock, Megaminx, Pyraminx, Skewb, Square-1 and FTO.
The owner chooses which timer types are allowed. Smart cube, GAN Timer and QiYi Timer require Pro inside rooms; keyboard, StackMat, QYtoys and manual entry are open to everyone.
If you would rather watch than solve, you can switch to spectator mode. Spectators do not hold up the round.
steps: Open a new room from the rooms page, or join an existing one with its link.
The owner picks the cube type and starts the round.
Your time is shared automatically when you finish. Once everyone in the room has solved, the next scramble arrives on its own.
If a wrong time gets recorded, you can correct or delete your most recent solve only. A corrected time shows a pencil mark in the table.
notes: There are three ranks: owner, moderator and participant. A moderator can kick and ban participants but cannot touch another moderator or the owner. Only the owner can appoint moderators and hand over the room.
Tap the round number, or any time in the table, to see that round's scramble again.
The owner or a moderator can reset the room from the menu. All solves and rounds are deleted, the cube type stays the same and everyone starts again from round 1.
A chat message can be at most 500 characters.
Playing music in a room requires Pro.

battle.title: Battle
body: Battle is a two-player duel on a single device. The screen splits in half, the far player's side is turned upside down, and two people sit facing each other and solve the same scramble. It works on phones, tablets and computers.
A round does not begin until both players hold the screen and go ready. Once both are ready, each player lifts their finger whenever they like and their own timer starts at that moment.
When a round ends the times stay on screen. The next round opens with a fresh scramble as soon as both players hold again.

Each player can also play with their own smart cube. That takes one smart cube per player; two players cannot share the same cube. One player can use a cube while the other taps the screen. Smart cubes in Battle do not need Pro.

A player with a connected cube applies their side's scramble to the cube. The moves are ticked off as they go, and once the scramble is done that side turns Ready. The timer starts with the first move and stops on its own when the cube is solved. Screen taps do not start or stop this player's timer.
steps: Open the Battle page and pick a cube type from the toolbar in the middle.
Both players hold their side of the screen; lift your fingers once both are ready.
Tap the screen to stop. Add a +2 or DNF penalty if you need to, and the score corrects itself.
Use the history button to review rounds, scrambles and who won.
notes: The menu lets you switch sides, get a new scramble, delete the last round or start a fresh battle.
The time, scramble, names, statistics, score and win streak displays can each be turned off on their own.
Battle rounds stay on the device and are not saved to your solve history.

To connect a smart cube, press Connect Cube on your side and pick your cube from the list. The two players connect their cubes one after the other. In a browser this needs Chrome or Edge; the iOS and Android apps have no such limit.
A cube connected on the timer page stays connected there. To use that same cube in Battle, disconnect it on the timer page first.
If the cube shows as scrambled when it connects, solve it first. If it is solved but shows as scrambled on screen, press Mark as solved in the cube button's menu.
When you switch sides, connected cubes move with their players, so there is no need to reconnect them.
On a computer without a touch screen, two players cannot hold at the same time. There, at least one player has to connect a smart cube.

online-battle.title: Online Battle
body: In Online Battle you play with your smart cube against another player who is searching at the same moment. You both solve the same scramble, and the first to win three rounds wins the match.
Time comes from the cube's own clock, so internet lag does not affect the result. After each match your rating changes and goes on the leaderboard.
You need to be signed in with a verified email. Only 3x3 for now.
steps: On the Battle page, tap the Online Battle card and connect your smart cube.
Press Find opponent. Once matched, you see how much your rating changes if you win or lose.

Apply the scramble on screen to your cube within 20 seconds; going over costs +2. Then 15 seconds of inspection start; your first move starts the time and solving the cube stops it. The solve limit is 60 seconds.
When the match ends, ask for a rematch or look for a new opponent.
notes: Only cubes with their own clock are accepted: GAN, QiYi and WeiLong V10 AI. Other smart cubes work in Offline Battle.
Leaving the match or giving up counts as a loss.
The same two players can play at most three rated matches a day; the rest are unrated.
For your first matches a question mark shows next to your rating. It settles after a few matches.
If your connection drops for a short while, the match waits for you.

messages.title: Messages
body: Messages is where you talk one to one with other Zkt Timer users. To start a conversation, search for a username and pick the person.

Someone writing to you for the first time does not land straight in your inbox; they wait in the Requests tab. Accept and the thread moves to your inbox. If you would rather not, you can delete it or block the person.
You can attach one of your solves to a conversation. The other person sees the time and can open the solve's detail.

Message settings live under Social in the account section: who is allowed to write to you, whether you appear in message search, read receipts, the typing indicator and the online dot. Your blocked list is kept there too.
steps: Press New message and start typing a username; search runs from two letters onward.
Write your message. Use the attach button if you want to share a solve.
You can edit a message you sent, or unsend it. Unsending removes it for the other person as well.
Report a conversation that bothers you, or block the person.
notes: Deleting a chat removes it from your side only; the other person keeps their copy.
When you report, a copy of the last five messages is sent for review. None of your other messages are read.
You can mute a conversation, filter the inbox down to unread, and search your history from the search box.

competitions.title: Competitions and rankings
body: The competitions page carries both WCA and Zeka Küpü Türkiye competitions. Upcoming competitions, ZKT competitions and the search box are all on the same page. If you linked your WCA account, your own registrations are listed separately under My Competitions.
Opening a competition gives you these tabs: Groups (the competitor list and assignments), live results, Events (rounds, formats and cutoffs), Rankings, Schedule (the whole programme) and Info.
ZKT competitions use the same page; only the live tab is named ZKT Live instead of WCA Live.
Tapping a competitor opens their schedule, groups and duties, with judging, running and scrambling shown separately. Their personal bests page is reachable from there too.
notes: The records section shows recently broken records. Getting record alerts, and following up to five competitors in a competition, requires Pro.

profile.title: Profile
body: Your profile is your public face on Zkt Timer. It lives at /user/yourusername and opens for anyone, signed in or not, so the link is all you need to share.
A cover photo and profile picture sit at the top, with the About section below: biography, YouTube, Twitch and X links, your 3x3 method, your goal, your main cube and your favourite event.

Records are split across tabs. Personal Records come from the solves you did in Zkt Timer. WCA Official Records and ZKT Records come from the accounts you linked. The WCA Results tab lists your competition history round by round.
Your times do not appear on the profile on their own. You pick which ones show, one by one, from the publish screen.
steps: Upload your profile picture and cover photo.
Open Edit Profile and fill in your biography, social links and cube details.
To publish personal records, set a username first, then choose the times you want to show.
If you linked a WCA or ZKT account, use Manage Data to choose what appears: competition count, medals, records, world ranking and competition history.
notes: Publishing your personal records on your profile requires Pro. Showing your WCA and ZKT records does not.
Create Cuber Card produces a shareable image that gathers your competition count, medals and records into one frame.
On someone else's profile you can send a message, copy the profile link and report them.

account.title: Account settings
body: The account page has seven sections: Personal Info, Notifications, Social, Linked Accounts, Announcements, Support and Danger Zone.

Personal Info is where you change your name, username and email, and set your password. An email change is confirmed with a six-digit code sent to the new address. If your account was created through WCA, this is also where you set a password so you can sign in with email as well.

Linked Accounts is where you connect your ZKT and WCA accounts. Once linked, that account's competitions, results and records become visible inside Zkt Timer. The link to join the WhatsApp community is here too.

Support is where you report a bug, ask a question or send a suggestion. A ticket works like a conversation: you can reply, attach a screenshot or video, close it once it is solved and reopen it later.
steps: For a support ticket, go to Support in the account section and write a subject and message.
After sending the ticket you can attach a screenshot or video to the conversation.
Turn on the email option under Notifications if you want to hear about replies by email.
Close the ticket once your issue is solved; you can reopen it later if you need to.
notes: One file per message, up to 25 MB. Images can be PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP; videos can be MP4, WebM or MOV.

The Danger Zone holds two actions. Resetting settings leaves your solves and sessions alone and does not touch your custom cube types; it only returns your settings to their defaults. Deleting your account erases all of your data permanently.
To unlink a connected account you need a password set first, otherwise you would be left with no way to sign in.

data.title: Data and backups
body: You can bring data in from these sources:
Go to Settings > Data > Import, pick the source and upload your file.
Export sits in the same place and writes all your solves, sessions and settings into one file.
While you are signed in, your solves are backed up to the server. The app keeps working without internet, and pending solves are sent once the connection comes back.
You can delete your account and all of your data permanently from the Danger Zone in the account section.

account_required.title: This section needs an account
account_required.stats: Statistics tie your solve history to your account: averages, records, an activity map and per-puzzle analysis. With an account, everything here fills up with your own data.
account_required.rooms: Rooms are for solving the same scramble as your friends. Times show up on everyone else's screen, which is why this one needs an identity.
account_required.trainer: The trainer keeps separate times and success rates for every algorithm, so the cases you are weak on rise to the top. That progress needs an account to live in.
account_required.trainer_sets: Your sets are saved to your account, so you see the same sets on every device. Sign in to build and save sets.
